clue.text: Fed up. Sir Thomas, with shed

parts.note: Sir Thomas Browne, the 17th-century English author of Religio Medici
to doff is to take off or shed, as one doffs a hat

explanation.surface: Someone is fed up with Sir Thomas and his garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: The full stop after 'Fed up' marks off the definition; 'shed' looks like a garden building but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A British slang expression for being bored and annoyed, much like 'fed up'.

clue.text: Money does attract this

explanation.surface: Cash is what draws people in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'does' is not the verb but the plural of doe: female deer attract the male of the species.
explanation.definitionFit: A dollar is slang-named after the male deer, and a male deer is what female deer draw to them in the rut.

clue.text: Gradual assimilation of big time girl

parts.note: OS is the abbreviation for outsize, i.e. very big
a mo is a moment, a short time
sis is short for sister, a girl in the family

explanation.surface: A big-time girl gradually absorbs everything around her.
explanation.definitionFit: The scientific term for liquid passing slowly through a membrane, used figuratively for taking in ideas little by little.

clue.text: Love acting? Certainly not!

parts.note: love is a zero score in tennis, i.e. nil
acting is performing or carrying out an activity

explanation.surface: Asked if they love acting, someone flatly refuses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' as zero comes from tennis scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial phrase of flat refusal, meaning 'no way'.

clue.text: Indeed, a bit late

indicators.note: read 'Indeed' as 'In deed': the word 'In' tells us a piece goes inside deed

parts.note: taken as written
a part is a bit of something

explanation.surface: Someone agrees that they are indeed a little behind time.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'Indeed' into 'In deed': 'a bit' (PART) goes inside DEED.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are euphemisms for someone who has died, as in 'the late king'.

clue.text: Calif's free of taxes

indicators.note: free signals that the letters are released from their order and rearranged

parts.note: the letters of Calif's, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: California, a state abbreviated Calif., has no taxes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free' looks like 'tax-free', but it is the anagram signal on CALIFS.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything to do with public revenue and taxation.

clue.text: Bill is a shepherd

parts.note: ac is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: A man named Bill works as a shepherd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but it is an account, AC.
explanation.definitionFit: In Ovid's myth he is the Sicilian shepherd loved by the sea-nymph Galatea.

clue.text: Draw together a large picture

explanation.surface: An artist draws a big picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To shut or bring together the sides of something, and a photograph taken from very near, filling the frame.

clue.text: Byway that's edged by straggling trees

annotationWithheld.why: Byway that's edged by straggling trees (4-6): SIDE + an anagram of TREES leaves STREET one T short, and 'edged by' gives SIDE only loosely; no clean parse found
annotationWithheld.clue: Byway that's edged by straggling trees

clue.text: Took place — as Xerxes did at Thermopylae

explanation.surface: History recalls the Persian king's march to the narrow pass.
explanation.walkthrough: Xerxes's Persian army marched up to the pass of Thermopylae, held by the Spartans in 480 BC.
explanation.definitionFit: An old phrase for happened, and literally the Persian king arriving at a mountain pass.

clue.text: An unpleasant character drawn to the audience

indicators.note: what is said to an audience is heard rather than read, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: drawn as in pulled along, towed

explanation.surface: A nasty villain is drawn to appeal to the theatre audience.
explanation.definitionFit: A loathsome person is called by the name of the warty amphibian.

clue.text: The man's conservative, without one term in the past

parts.note: his means belonging to the man

indicators.note: without in the old sense of outside, so the Tory wraps round the rest

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party
I is the Roman numeral one
to term something is to name or call it

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician is out of office after one term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here, not lacking: TORY goes round I + CALL.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means with reference to former times, as in long ago.

clue.text: Wine — it's twice rejected

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: the word 'it' is used twice: once as it is, and once as SA, sex appeal, which 'it' means in old slang
the word 'it' is used twice: once as it is, and once as SA, sex appeal, which 'it' means in old slang

explanation.surface: A wine has twice been sent back by a diner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' means sex appeal (SA) in old slang; IT + SA read backwards gives the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A sparkling Italian white from Piedmont.

clue.text: Being prepared to study one such as 29

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it
I is the Roman numeral one
the clue numbered 29 names a headland, and a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A student gets ready to study a famous landmark.
explanation.walkthrough: 29's answer is a chalk headland on England's south coast; a ness is a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means a state of being ready for something.

clue.text: A state payment's very little money for a youth

parts.note: the dole is state unemployment benefit in Britain, here with its 's
a cent is a very small coin

explanation.surface: Welfare for a young person amounts to almost nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The dole is British slang for state unemployment benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: A teenager, someone between childhood and adulthood.

clue.text: Argue about entering the lady's age

parts.note: Di, a woman's name, with its 's

indicators.note: entering means going into, so one piece is placed inside the word age

parts.note: taken as written
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Two people argue about whether to mention a woman's age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is RE, not a container signal; 'entering' puts it inside AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To quarrel or differ in opinion.

clue.text: The dullness of Proust's characters

indicators.note: characters as letters of the name, taken out of their order and rearranged

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A critic complains about the dullness of the people in Proust's novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' looks like people in the novels; it means the letters of PROUST, rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A dazed, torpid state of mind, near unconsciousness.

clue.text: Variety of conifers used in courts

indicators.note: a variety is a different form, so the letters of the word take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A kind of pine tree is used to furnish courtrooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variety of' looks like a botanist's phrase but signals an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes evidence or science applied in law courts.

clue.text: The letter S heard and seen in 'Gosh'

indicators.note: seen in means appearing inside, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: lor is an old exclamation of surprise, like 'Lord!'
the letter S as spoken is spelt out ess

explanation.surface: The letter S appears when you say 'Gosh'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The letter' is not a character of the alphabet but one who lets out property.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlord who leases property is one who lets it.

clue.text: Bag carried by pensioners at Chelsea

indicators.note: carried by means held within, so the answer sits inside these words

explanation.surface: Retired soldiers in Chelsea carry bags.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea Pensioners are retired soldiers living at the Royal Hospital in Chelsea, London.
explanation.definitionFit: A school bag with a shoulder strap.

clue.text: Stretch the food

explanation.surface: Someone eats slowly to make the meal last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch' is British slang for a prison sentence, as is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a term in prison, and oatmeal boiled for breakfast.

clue.text: Intend to tie ends loosely

indicators.note: loosely suggests the knot is slack, so the letters fall out of order

explanation.surface: Someone means to tie the loose ends of a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: To ordain or mean something for a purpose.

clue.text: In punishment it is limited

indicators.note: In tells us the word it goes inside the punishment

parts.note: a fine is a monetary punishment

explanation.surface: Punishment is limited by law.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means having bounds, not endless.

clue.text: Light switch is not free

indicators.note: switch as a verb means swap round, so the letters change places

explanation.surface: A light switch costs money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light switch' looks like one thing; 'Light' is the definition and 'switch' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To light a fire is to kindle or ignite it.

clue.text: Covering the action

explanation.surface: Someone takes cover from what is going on.
explanation.definitionFit: A box or container that encloses something, and a lawsuit brought in court.

clue.text: Urge forward without fighting

parts.note: pro means for or in favour of

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letters of the next word are removed

parts.note: taken as written
war is fighting

explanation.surface: Someone presses ahead peacefully.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'forward' into 'for ward': PRO + WARD, with WAR (fighting) taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: To poke or push someone into action.

clue.text: The girl to make a comeback

explanation.surface: A young woman returns to the spotlight.
explanation.walkthrough: The girl is the nymph of Greek myth who wasted away until only her voice remained.
explanation.definitionFit: A mythical nymph, and to sound back as a reflected voice does.

clue.text: Toy retailed in much smaller case

indicators.note: in tells us the word for retailed goes inside, the other word acting as its case

parts.note: tinier means much smaller
retailed means sold in a shop

explanation.surface: A toy was sold in a much smaller box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' completes the container signal 'in ... case': SOLD goes inside TINIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A small metal figure of a soldier, a classic toy.

clue.text: Where to keep the money — it's about two pounds

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: the word it, with 's as a link
L is the abbreviation for a pound, twice

explanation.surface: A cash box holds about two pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: The cash drawer in a shop counter.

clue.text: Dispatch contains painful point

indicators.note: contains means holds inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: to dispatch is to kill, as to behead
achy means aching, painful

explanation.surface: A message holds a painful point.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a chalk headland on England's south coast in Sussex; 'point' means a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: A headland jutting into the sea, as a promontory does.
